participating-org.narrative:
Nature Talk Africa (NaTA) is a community youth-led, non-profit organization based in Hoima district, mid-western region Uganda. Theorganization was founded in 2023 and was registered in 2024 by Hoima District Local Government as a community-based organization. The majority of the youth in Nature Talk Africa are those who have been affected by the ongoing oil development activities in our communities of Hoima and Kikuube districts from a young age. Witnessing first-hand the socio-economic injustices that have been resulting due to the development triggered us after acquiring some education in different fields; education, social work/sciences, community development, agriculture, human rights law among others to organize ourselves to contribute to our community efforts in promoting respect of our community rights, sustainable community livelihoods development, climate justice, nature conservation and protection amidst the ongoing oil development activities. Nature Talk Africa was co-founded by two community youth in May, 2023. In August, 2023 more 6 community youth from Kikuube and Hoima joined the technical team, and we work jointly with the Oil Refinery Residents Association (ORRA) team on a campaign to reactivate indigenous knowledge and amplifying local voices in climate action (Nature Talk Africa manages all the youth related work). In May, 2024, Nature Talk Africa was registered as a community-based organization by the Hoima District Local Government. Nature Talk Africa has its membership now extended to Buliisa district, we currently have one community youth coordinator in each of the three districts where we work and we are hosted by ORRA which is an umbrella organization that brings together oil and gas project affected persons. 2.ACHIEVEMENTS Over the last two year Nature Talk Africa has made significant contributions towards empowering local youth climate and human rights activists, fostering economic resilience, and strengthening advocacy efforts to address injustice, exclusion and resilience within the oil host communities.We have built strong collaborations with community-based organizations such as ORRA and EACOP Host Communities (EACOP HC), as well as national and international organizations like Fridays for Future Uganda, Youth for Green Communities, Tree adoption Uganda among others.These partnerships have enhanced our ability to mobilize youth climate activists and environmental human rights defenders to stand up against the injustices caused by the ongoing oil and gas development in our community. Through non-violent direct actions, including petitions and peaceful marches, we have amplified community demands for justice. Notably, the March to Hoima High Court on April 15, 2024, advocated for delayed court decisions affecting Refinery Project-Affected Persons, while the August 26, 2024, march to EACOP and PAU offices in Hoima and Kampala demanded greater transparency and accountability in oil developments. We trained over 40 youth climate activists from Buliisa, Hoima, and Kikuubedistricts on effective advocacy tips including use of social media platforms like X which significantly strengthened their ability to speak out on environmental and community rights. We have supported sustainable, agriculture-based livelihood initiativesin several villages, ensuring long-term community resilience amidst the increasing effects of climate change. In Nyakasinina, Kwaki, Ngemwa, Nyahaira, and Kitegwa villages (Kabalale sub-county, Hoima district), we have facilitated over 150 youth, women,and men to engage in alternative income-generating activities, including fish and vegetable farming as well as beekeeping community projects. Beyond economic empowerment, our work has fostered a strong and supportive environment among oil-affected personsin Hoima, Buliisa, and Kikuube districts. Through continuous engagement, we have built trust and solidarity with displaced and affected communities, creating platforms for dialogue where people can collectively raise concerns and demand action from authorities.
3.INSTITUTIONAL PURPOSE We envision a resilient and sustainable community where nature and people flourish. Mission: To provide inclusive innovative approaches to community development, local climate change adaptation and protection of youth and environmental rights.
Institutional objectives: i. To enhance communities’ resilience and adaptive capacity to climate change impacts. ii. To promote gender equity and inclusiveness in environmental conservation, community developments and local climate actions. iii. To promote inclusive and sustainable community livelihood development initiatives. Field(s) of activity:
Nature Talk Africa works with youth on human rights issues, environmental conservation, climate change advocacy and community livelihood development in the Albertine Region of Uganda where major oil and gas development activities are taking place.
4. STRATEGIC POSITIONING Our organization operates in a complex environment shaped by oil development activities in the Bunyoro sub-region. The key stakeholders in this space include government line ministries, oil companies, and local businesses, each playing distinct roles. What sets us apart is that our staff is primarily composed of individuals who have been directly affected by oil developments. This lived experience strengthens our connection with communities in Hoima, Buliisa, and Kikuube districts, particularly those impacted by projects such as the Refinery, Tilenga, Kingfisher, and EACOP oil projects. Our deep rootedties enable us to work closely with oil-affected communities and advocate effectively for our concerns. We actively engage with local government leaders, including village-level Local Councils (LC 1 to LC III), Community Development Officers (CDOs), andDistrict Community Development Officers (DCDOs). These officials play a critical role in our work, often participating in our meetings where they interact directly with community members, listen to their concerns, and provide facilitative support during community convenings. Our unique position as an organization stems from our grassroots-driven approach, our direct ties to affected communities, and our ability to bridge the gap between local communities, government institutions, and other stakeholders in the oil sector.
